titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Tuesday, 1 March 1921
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Miss Weaver: LIII 39-40 A fortnight ago when nearly 100 pages of Circe (about half) were typed the father of my typist had a seizure in the street (a Circean episode, as it happens) and consequently the work came to an end. Now a fair copy is made from my MS and then passed on to another typist who will finish the episode slowly. I sent the first half of Eumeus to still another typist and I am told it is almost finished. I am writing out the fair copy of the end of it and shall send it on in a few days.

I am now working on Ithaca. This episode and Penelope will take all my time till May. As I needed for both of them my notes left in Trieste I have been writing express registered letters to my relatives there and certain friends without any success till yesterday when I got a letter saying that a person who is coming to Paris ‘shortly’ will bring them.

I have not seen Mr Aldington’s article in the English Review . Possibly it is in the March number. I do not know his address. If I did I should write to him to ask him to send me back a dossier of documents which Mr Pound posted on to him. I believe that Mr Pound has left London though I do not know where he is at present.

I have no news from New York either of the trial or of the publication nor do I know whether the Little Review is still in existence or not. There is also no news about the French version of my novel except for a long hysterical letter from the translator defending herself against rumours of neglect and incompetence. Perhaps I ought to say that the book was given to her to translate by Mr Pound before my arrival in Paris. I do not know how much English she knows but on looking at one of her pages by chance I found that she does not know that ‘Gugusse’ is the short name for ‘Guillaume’. To find an equivalent for this you must imagine an English writer who does not know that ‘Billy’ is the short for ‘William’. At the same time I should not like this to be known to her discredit as I am informed that she has a literary reputation of some sort and, apart from that, I know that she is neurasthenic on account of family complications.

seg.quote: I have at least one item of news which is not bad.

div.note: “The Influence of Mr. James Joyce”, English Review (April 1921): 333-41.

An official complaint for obscenity had been filed against the New York magazine The Little Review for publishing the July-August 1920 number containing the portion of the “Nausicaa” episode of Ulysses in which Leopold Bloom masturbates at the seashore (LIII 27-28). For fuller accounts of “Nausicaa” and the prosecution and trial it occasioned, see JJ to Pound, 24 October 1919, notes; 5 November 1920, notes; and 16 November 1920, notes.

As JJ writes, it was indeed Pound who suggested that Ludmila Savitzky translate A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man into French. The translation appeared in 1924 as Dedalus: Portrait de l'artiste jeune par lui-même (Paris: Éditions de la Sirène), following a difficult search for a publisher and some antagonism between author and translator. See Leonid Livak's “‘A Thankless Occupation’: James Joyce and His Translator Ludmila Savitzky”, Joyce Studies Annual (2013): 33-61. Despite JJ's criticism, Savitzky's translation remained the standard in French for decades.
In French, the short name for “Guillaume” is “Gugusse”, meaning clown. Thanks to Daniel Ferrer for assistance with the French.
